1.1 Principle:

High-performance liquid chromatography (USP <621>)

1.2 Reagents:

Reference substances: CP-6 standard

Buffer: Approx. 27.2 mg/ml KH2PO4 in water, pH 5.0 adjusted by addition of NaOH solution 2M

Diluent: Acetonitrile: Phosphate Buffer (1:4)

Blank: Take 5 ml of Acetonitrile and dilute to 50 ml with Diluent

1.3 Chromatography

Column:                    length 250 mm, internal diameter 4.6 mm

Stationary phase:    Silica C 18, 3.5 µm, e.g. Nucleosil 250-C 18, 3.5µm

System:                     isocratic

Mobile Phase:          Acetonitrile / Phosphate Buffer (40:60)

Flow rate:                  1.0 mL/min

Oven temperature:  30 ± 1 °C

Sample injection:     10 µl

Detection:                 UV, 230 nm

Evaluation: Integration of the peaks referring to product; comparison of the retention times of test and reference solution.

1.4 Procedure:

Test solution: Approximately 0.1 mg/ml of sample to be examined in diluent.

Reference solution: Approximately 0.1 mg/ml of CP-8 standard in diluent.

1.5 System Suitability Test

Theoretical plates: In the chromatogram of five replicate injections of reference solution, the number of theoretical plates is higher than 3200.

Reproducibility: In the chromatogram of reference solution, the relative standard deviation between peak areas of replicate injections (five injections) is not more than 0.73 %.

1.6 Calculation

The content of CP-6 is calculated according to the following formula:

[IMAGE: Untitled.png]

AM =   Peak area value of CP-6 in the test solution

AS =    Peak area value of CP-6 in the reference solution

CS =    Weight of CP-6 (mg) in the reference solution

CM =   Weight of CP-6 (mg) in the test solution

V =      Assay of CP-6 standard, in %

Report the result “as is”.

3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

For determination of assay of Sakuramil an HPLC method was developed and validated by IROHA-corp. The method is validated in terms of specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, intermediate precision, system suitability and stability of the test solutions.

2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary

In the present report, validation results of the assay test (HPLC) as described in DMF section [[2.3.4.AP Analytical Procedures (Assay/ID) [Assay/Identification] [Sakuramil]]] are compiled and evaluated.

For assay determination by HPLC, specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, intermediate precision, system suitability and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures.

Following acceptance criteria have been defined in a method validation protocol.

Table 2‑1 Acceptance criteria

Validation ParameterAcceptance CriteriaResults
Specificity / System Suitability Requirements· Analyte peak of CP-9 is sufficiently separated from all other peaks; no peak is interfering with the CP-9 peak (Resolution ≥ 2.0) · Theoretical Plates (n=5): > 3200 · Reproducibility (n=5): ≤ 0.73 %· Resolution = 12.1 · Theoretical Plates = 5686 · Reproducibility = 0.18 %
Solution StabilityChange in assay within specified time relative to the initial value: ≤ 1.0 %During the tested time period the relative change of CP-9 peak areas is within respective acceptance criterion (≤ 1.0 %).
LinearityBy visual inspection, the residuals/responses are randomly distributed Correlation coefficient : R ≥ 0.998 Y-intercept : ≤ 2.0 % Residual standard deviation : ≤ 2.0 %The residuals/responses are randomly distributed Correlation coefficient = R 1.0459 Y-intercept = 0.9997 % Residual standard deviation = 0.060 %
Range· Minimum 60 to 130 % target concentration ·  If acceptance criteria for linearity are fulfilled, range of the method is demonstrated.The method has been validated for a range of 60% to 130% of the concentration examined (0.1 mg/ml of Sakuramil)

Intermediate Precisionn ≥ 12; RSD ≤ 1.0 %n = 12; RSD = 0.3 %

Individual recovery rates between 97-103 %RSD (n=6) = 0.003 - 0.004 % Recovery between 99.9 and 100.1 %

Evaluation of the results confirmed that this HPLC method is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameters specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision as well as stability of the solutions could be demonstrated. Furthermore, the required system suitability criteria for theoretical plates and reproducibility fulfill the respective acceptance criteria. Therefore, also accuracy of the method could be confirmed under the actual conditions of use.

text.div:
3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description

Purpose and scope

This procedure is used to detect and quantify ICH-M7 alerting, process-related impurities CP-3, CP-4 and CP-5 in the drug substance (Sakuramil) for confirmatory testing to verify the purge argument that supports Option 3 per ICH M7.

Analytical principle

Quantification is performed by reversed-phase LC coupled to mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) using electrospray ionization in positive mode and multiple-reaction monitoring (MRM). The LC separation provides selectivity against matrix components; MS/MS provides sensitivity at sub-ppm levels.

Typical conditions (representative; exact tuned values are recorded in the method record AP-MI-LCMS-01)

• Column: C18, ~100 × 2.1 mm, ~1.7–3 µm.

• Mobile phases: A = water with ~0.1% formic acid; B = acetonitrile with ~0.1% formic acid.

• Gradient: initial 5–10% B to 90–95% B in ~8–10 min; total run ≤ 15 min.

• Flow/temperature/injection: ~0.30 mL·min⁻¹ / 35–45 °C / 2–10 µL.

• Detection: MRM transitions individually optimized for CP-3, CP-4, CP-5; qualifier/quantifier ion-ratio acceptance ±20% of calibrator at comparable response.

• Internal standard (IS): a stable-isotope-labelled or suitable structural analogue; single-point IS normalization is used for drift and matrix-effect correction.

Solutions and sample preparation

• Stock standards: ~0.1 mg/mL of each impurity in acetonitrile.

• Mixed working standards: prepare at ~0.3×, 0.5×, 1.0×, and 1.5× of the reporting level (see below).

• Sample: dissolve API to ~10 mg/mL in water:acetonitrile (1:1, v/v), spike with IS, vortex, and filter (0.22 µm PTFE or PVDF; filter-compatibility verified).

• Matrix-matched calibration: performed in API matrix (blank API demonstrated free of targets) to mitigate matrix effects.

System suitability

Prior to analysis:

• S/N at the LOQ standard ≥ 10 (each analyte).

• Peak tailing ≤ 2.0 for all targets; IS-normalized area RSD for five replicate injections ≤ 10%.

• MRM ion-ratio criteria met for standards and samples (±20% window).

Reportable units and limits

Results are reported as µg/g (ppm) relative to API. The analytical reporting level is set at or below the M7 acceptable-intake-based limit (AI/MDD), and, for this product, has been fixed at ≤ 10 ppm (individual) to align with the purge-verification strategy; the method is designed to achieve LOQ ≤ 30% of the reporting level (≤ 3 ppm) and typically achieves ≤ 1 ppm for all three impurities.

> Note on control strategy: > > > CP-3 (formed in situ), CP-4 (starting material) and CP-5 (in situ intermediate) are controlled upstream (e.g., CP-4 spec NMT 0.3%, CP-6 spec NMT 0.1%) and by demonstrated purge to < 10 ppm in the final API. Confirmatory testing of the first three commercial API batches and periodic verification (skip-lot) are performed with this LC–MS/MS method. >

3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

Validation was performed in line with ICH Q2(R2) terminology and principles and, where relevant, the method design/knowledge elements of ICH Q14 (e.g., deliberate variability studies to establish a robust operating region). Unless stated otherwise, acceptance criteria follow common practice for M7 trace analysis: LOQ ≤ 30% of the reporting level; trueness 80–120% (≥ 70–130% at LOQ); repeatability RSD ≤ 15% (≤ 20% at LOQ); coefficient of determination (R) ≥ 0.99. A full data package is available in report AP-VAL-MI-Sakura-01.

Selectivity/Identification capability

• No interfering peaks at the retention times of CP-3, CP-4, CP-5 or IS in reagent blank, placebo, or API matrix.

• MRM qualifier/quantifier ion ratios in samples met ±20% acceptance versus standards at similar responses, confirming identity.

Calibration model and working range

• Matrix-matched calibration over 0.3× to 1.5× of the reporting level using ≥ 5 levels (plus LOQ).

• Weighted (1/x) linear regression; R ≥ 0.99 for all analytes; back-calculated levels within ±15% (±20% at LOQ).

Detection capability (LOD/LOQ)

• LOQ established by S/N ≥ 10 and precision/trueness criteria; achieved LOQs ≤ 1 ppm for CP-3, CP-4, CP-5 (≤ 10% of the 10-ppm reporting level).

• LOD estimated as ~⅓ of LOQ (S/N ≥ 3).

Trueness (recovery) and precision

• Trueness: triplicate spike-recoveries at LOQ, 0.5×, 1.0× across three API batches: 98–107% (LOQ: 90–110%).

• Repeatability: six independent preparations at the reporting level: RSD ≤ 6%.

• Intermediate precision: different day/analyst/instrument: RSD ≤ 10% at the reporting level; ≤ 15% at LOQ.

System suitability acceptance criteria (for routine use)

• S/N (LOQ) ≥ 10; IS-normalized peak-area RSD (n=5) ≤ 10%; retention-time RSD ≤ 2%; ion-ratio within ±20% of calibrator.

3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

For determination of potentially mutagenic impurities of Sakuramil an HPLC method was developed and validated by IROHA-corp. The method is validated in terms of specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy, robustness, system suitability and stability of the test solutions.

2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary

In the present report, validation results of the determination of potentially mutagenic impurities (HPLC) as described in DMF section [[2.3.3.AP Analytical Procedures (Potentially mutagentic Impurities) [Potentially mutagenic Impurities] [Sakuramil]]] are compiled and evaluated.

The method considers the specified impurity from Sakuramil drug substance as well as total impurities. The specified impurity as per DMF section [[2.3.3.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] is CP-6.

The analytical procedure can be stated validated in accordance with ICH Q2(R2) and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

For determination of potentially mutagenic impurities by HPLC, specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), system suitability and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures.

Evaluation of Recorded Spectra:

• Each of these spectra is compared with the average spectrum (n = 5) of the chromatographic peak. Correspondence is expressed via a similarity factor with values between 1000 (identical spectra) and 0 (no match).

• The plot of similarity factors along the chromatographic peak gives the similarity curve.

• A purity factor is calculated taking both the similarity and threshold values into account (values between 1000 and 0).

Calculation of the Peak Purity:

• The mean of all purity values gives the purity factor (= match factor).

• The match factor is calculated for the CP-9 peak as well as for impurity peaks > 0.10 %.

Acceptance Criteria Stability-Indicating Testing / Peak Purity:

• adequate selectivity is given

• observed level > 70.0 % → match factor ≥ 995.0

• observed level > 5.0 % → match factor ≥ 950.0

• observed level > 0.5 % → match factor ≥ 900.0

• observed level > 0.1 % → match factor ≥ 800.0

2.4 Conclusion

Evaluation of the results confirmed that the HPLC method used for determination of related substances in Sakuramil is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameter specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy and robustness as well as stability indicating capability fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.

Robustness of the method with regards to variation of following chromatographic conditions is given:

• column temperature: 23 to 30 °C

• flow rate: 1.1 to 1.3 mL/min

• pH of eluents: 4.8 to 5.0

• variation of column lot

Additionally, the stability of reference solution and test solution stored at RT have been demonstrated. A possible holdup time of at least 28 hours was defined for the reference solution and of maximum of 20 hours for the test solution, respectively.

Furthermore, following response correction factors in relation to Sakuramil (RCFs to be multiplied with) were determined:

CP-6=1.19

From evaluation of the data following system suitability test criteria were defined:

Resolution: In the chromatogram of the reference solution, the resolution between the peaks of CP-6 and CP-9 is not less than 1.5.

Reproducibility: In the chromatogram of reference solution, the relative standard deviation between peak areas of replicate injections (six injections) of CP-9 is not more than 1.0%.

The analytical procedure can be stated validated and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

For determination of related substances of Sakuramil an HPLC method was developed and validated by IROHA-corp. The method is validated in terms of specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy, robustness, system suitability and stability of the test solutions.

2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary

In the present report, validation results of the determination of related substances test (HPLC) as described in DMF section [[2.3.3.AP Analytical Procedures (Related Substances)[Purity][Sakuramil]]] are compiled and evaluated.

The method considers all specified impurities from Sakuramil drug substance as well as unspecified impurities. Specified impurities as per DMF section [[2.3.3.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] are CP-8 and CP-9-1.

The analytical procedure can be stated validated in accordance with ICH Q2(R2) and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

For determination of related substances by HPLC, specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), system suitability and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures.

Following acceptance criteria have been defined in a method validation protocol.

Evaluation of Recorded Spectra:

• Each of these spectra is compared with the average spectrum (n = 5) of the chromatographic peak. Correspondence is expressed via a similarity factor with values between 1000 (identical spectra) and 0 (no match).

• The plot of similarity factors along the chromatographic peak gives the similarity curve.

• A purity factor is calculated taking both the similarity and threshold values into account (values between 1000 and 0).

Calculation of the Peak Purity:

• The mean of all purity values gives the purity factor (= match factor).

• The match factor is calculated for the CP-9 peak as well as for impurity peaks > 0.10 %.

Acceptance Criteria Stability-Indicating Testing / Peak Purity:

• adequate selectivity is given

• observed level > 70.0 % → match factor ≥ 995.0

• observed level > 5.0 % → match factor ≥ 950.0

• observed level > 0.5 % → match factor ≥ 900.0

2.3.13.12 Conclusion of forced degradation study

Forced degradation study results showed that the chromatographic methods for determination of related substances and assay are stability indicating with respect to the described conditions. No relevant increase of related substances was observed when the substance was exposed to light stress (conditions according to ICH Q1B). Thus, the product can be considered photostable. No interference of degradation products with known by-products was detected (apart from conditions in presence of copper(III) ions). The largest unknown degradation product was observed at oxidative conditions (12.48 % at RT 5.50).

2.4 Conclusion

Evaluation of the results confirmed that the HPLC method used for determination of related substances in Sakuramil is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameter specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy and robustness as well as stability indicating capability fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.

Robustness of the method with regards to variation of following chromatographic conditions is given:

• column temperature: 23 to 30 °C

• flow rate: 1.1 to 1.3 mL/min

• pH of eluents: 4.8 to 5.0

• variation of column lot

Additionally, the stability of reference solution and test solution stored at RT have been demonstrated. A possible holdup time of at least 28 hours was defined for the reference solution and of maximum of 20 hours for the test solution, respectively.

Furthermore, following response correction factors in relation to Sakuramil (RCFs to be multiplied with) were determined:

CP-9-1=  1.23

CP-8= 2.01

From evaluation of the data following system suitability test criteria were defined:

Resolution: In the chromatogram of the identification solution, the resolution between the peaks of CP-8 and CP-9, and CP-9-1 and CP-9 is not less than 1.5.

Reproducibility: In the chromatogram of reference solution, the relative standard deviation between peak areas of replicate injections (six injections) of CP-9 is not more than 1.0%.

Forced degradation study results showed that the chromatographic methods for determination of related substances and assay are stability indicating with respect to the described conditions.

The analytical procedure can be stated validated and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

For the determination of residual solvents, a compendial GC method (USP <467> Procedure A) is used. The method is verified in accordance with USP <1467> Residual Solvents – Verification of compendial procedures and validation of alternative procedures. Verification of compendial methods for limit tests like Residual solvents includes the parameters specificity, detection limit (LOD) and solution stability.

2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary

In the present report, verification results of the determination of residual solvents test (GC) as described in USP <467> Procedure A are compiled and evaluated.

The method considers the specified residual solvent from Sakuramil drug substance. Specified residual solvent as per DMF section [[2.3.3.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] is Dichloromethane. Additionally, the method is used for determination of the IPC Ethanol (IPC #2).

The analytical procedure can be stated validated in accordance with ICH Q2(R2) and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

For determination of residual solvents by GC, specificity, limit of detection (LOD) and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to USP <1467> Residual Solvents—Verification of Compendial Procedures and Validation of Alternative Procedures and current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures. USP <1467> is focusing on Class 1 and 2 solvents, however, the same procedure was applied for Ethanol determination in order to ensure that the method is suitable under actual conditions of use.

Following acceptance criteria have been defined in a method verification protocol.

A reverse phase gradient HPLC method for the assay, related substances and degradation product CP-9-1 of Sakura Bloom in 20 mg Film-coated tablets was validated as per the method validation protocol VP_SB_21_2021.  The validated parameters include specificity, linearity, recovery, solution stability, precision, and robustness/ruggedness.  Additionally, filter absorption and completeness of extraction was also evaluated.  The validation results presented in the report VR_SB_21_2021, presented below, show that the method is specific, linear, accurate, precise, robust and stability indicating.

3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description

Dissolution under RTRT is controlled in three-dimensional design space so that the dissolution is about 90% (feedback control of spray rate by FBRM, compression force control by compression force controller).

1) Particle size of drug substance affecting dissolution is a specification item for drug substance which is performed by Laser diffraction particle size distribution analyzer.

2) Granule particle size is monitored using Focused Beam Reflectance Measurement (FBRM).

3) Uncoated tablet hardness is controlled by tablet hardness tester.

The particle size of drug substance is measured as a specification testing in the process of drug substance, by a laser diffraction-scattering type particle size distribution measuring device. Without preparing samples for measurement, the powder of drug substance is measured for particle distribution by the dry method (specification testing of drug substance). Regarding the particle size of the granulation, the particle size at the end of granulation, which is obtained by a FBRM method is used. The uncoated tablet hardness is measured in 200 tablets (10 tablets × 20 time points) sampled over time.

Dissolution test was performed for the drug product manufactured under the conditions allocated by DoE, and the affect of each factor on the dissolution rate were investigated. The test results were subjected to multidimensional analysis. For the formula for the sum of each factor which is multiplied by a coefficient, the coefficients that make the residual sum of squares minimum were calculated (the formula is shown below).

The dissolution rate calculated by the dissolution model at the time point of 30 minutes is 80% or higher.

[IMAGE: Untitled.png]

By controlling each process using this system, dissolution of the drug product is considered to be assured.

3.2.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development

1. Objective

To develop a Real-Time Release Testing (RTRT) method for monitoring and predicting the dissolution behavior of pharmaceutical solid dosage forms using ultraviolet (UV) spectroscopy.

---

2. Principle

UV spectroscopy measures the absorbance of UV light by a drug substance in solution. The absorbance at specific wavelengths correlates with the concentration of the dissolved active pharmaceutical ingredient (API), enabling real-time monitoring of dissolution.

---

3. Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs)

• Primary CQA: Dissolution rate

• Supporting CQAs:

• API concentration in solution

• Absorbance at characteristic UV wavelengths

• pH and temperature of dissolution medium

---

4. Process Analytical Technology (PAT) Tools
PAT ToolPurpose
UV SpectrophotometerReal-time monitoring of API concentration in dissolution medium
pH and Temperature ProbesControl and monitor dissolution conditions
Flow-through Cell or Fiber Optic ProbeIn-situ sampling and measurement

---

5. Predictive Modeling Approach

• Model Type: Calibration curve or multivariate regression (e.g., PLS)

• Input Variables: Absorbance values at selected wavelengths, time, pH, temperature

• Output Variable: Dissolution profile (concentration vs. time)

• Model Basis: Beer-Lambert Law:

A=ε⋅c⋅lA=ε⋅c⋅l

where:

• AA: absorbance

• εε: molar absorptivity

• cc: concentration

• ll: path length

---

6. Method Development Steps

• Wavelength Selection: Identify optimal wavelength(s) for API detection.

• Calibration Curve: Prepare standard solutions and generate absorbance vs. concentration curve.

• Dissolution Testing: Conduct dissolution studies with in-line UV monitoring.

• Model Building: Correlate real-time absorbance data with dissolution profiles.

• Validation: Validate the method per ICH Q2(R2) for accuracy, precision, linearity, and robustness.

• Implementation: Integrate UV probe into dissolution apparatus for RTRT.

---

7. Regulatory Considerations

• Follow USP <711> for dissolution testing and USP <857> for UV-Vis spectroscopy.

• Ensure proper calibration and maintenance of UV equipment.

• Validate the method for specificity, especially in the presence of excipients or degradation products.

The dissolution method (Dissolution by UV) for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is described in validation protocol VP_SB_22_2021 has been validated for full development. Details are reported in:

3.2.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development

The method was designed to ensure biorelevant in vitro performance and consistent results across manufacturing batches.

1. Solubility and Media Selection

Sakuramil is a white solid with low aqueous solubility at room temperature (0.05 mg/mL in water). Solubility varies significantly with pH:

• pH 1.2 (0.1 N HCl): < 0.1 mg/mL

• pH 4.5 (acetate buffer): 5.0 mg/mL

• pH 6.8 (phosphate buffer): 3.2 mg/mL

• pH 8.0 (0.1 N NaOH): 5.1 mg/mL

These results confirm sink conditions at physiological pH and justify the selection of McIlvaine buffer pH 5.0 as the dissolution medium.

2. Apparatus and Test Conditions

Comparative testing using USP Apparatus I (Basket) and II (Paddle) was performed. Apparatus II (Paddle) at 50 ± 2 rpm provided consistent and reproducible results with minimal variability. Use of sinkers was evaluated and found unnecessary. Filter compatibility was assessed, and a suitable material was selected to ensure sample clarity without adsorbing the drug substance.

The standard volume recommended by the USP for the dissolution testing of immediate release products is 900 mL; therefore, this dissolution volume was selected.

During the development phase, sampling timepoints of 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, and 45 were set to adequately characterize the ascending and plateau phases of the dissolution curves. More than 85% of the drug is released within the duration of the dissolution test.

[IMAGE: attachment:10a6a9a7-30d7-4b13-a084-c37a6da246dd:image.png]

[IMAGE: attachment:243125dd-a6fa-41f9-b6d6-a434547e0af8:image.png]

3. Discriminating ability of the dissolution method

The method’s discriminatory capability was confirmed by testing batches with deliberate formulation, and process variations. The procedure successfully detected differences in dissolution behavior, validating its suitability for stability studies and quality control.

[IMAGE: attachment:24155775-30cc-4438-a64e-47e27a097e7e:image.png]

[IMAGE: attachment:4601e31b-9634-4bdf-824e-444223fb9273:image.png]

4. Deaeration

Deaeration of the medium was evaluated and found to have no impact on dissolution results under the selected conditions. Therefore, deaeration is not required for routine testing.

5. Target Q Value

In accordance with pharmacopoeial guidance, the target Q value was defined as not less than 80% of the labeled amount dissolved within the specified time frame. This specification was supported by data from the batches used in the clinical trials and confirmed during method validation.

[IMAGE: attachment:29d4fdb4-69ce-4e84-8a6d-7ca63453f020:image.png]

6. Final Method Conditions

The finalized method is based on ultraviolet absorption spectroscopy and follows the principles outlined in Ph. Eur. 2.9.3, USP, and JP 6.10. The test is performed using Apparatus II (Paddle) at 50 ± 2 rpm in 900 mL of McIlvaine buffer (pH 5.0), prepared by dissolving sodium phosphate dibasic dihydrate and citric acid in 800 mL of demineralized water, adjusting pH with HCl or NaOH, and completing the volume to 1 L with distilled water. The dissolution temperature is maintained at 37 ± 0.5 °C.

A minimum of six units are tested, one per vessel, in accordance with the acceptance criteria of Ph. Eur., USP, and JP. UV detection is used to determine the absorbance of the test solutions, with reference solutions prepared at approximately 0.25 mg/mL of Sakuramil. Absorbance values are measured using a suitable spectrophotometer, and comparative evaluation is performed when applicable.

7. Conclusion

The dissolution method developed for

Sakura Bloom 20 mg

is scientifically justified, robust, and compliant with international pharmacopoeial standards. It demonstrates reproducibility, discriminatory power, and suitability for routine quality control, comparative dissolution studies, and regulatory submissions. The incorporation of UV detection and McIlvaine buffer at pH 5.0 ensures reliable performance and sensitivity across batches, supporting product quality throughout its shelf life.

3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description

Principle

Isocratic Reverse Phase HPLC with UV detection at 218 nm

Reagents
WaterDouble deionized and filtered, e.g. Milli-Q
AcetonitrileHPLC grade, e.g. Merck no. 1.00030, or equivalent
Potassium dihydrogen phosphate, anhydrousACS reagent grade, Aldrich Chemical no. 22130-9, or equivalent
Ammonium hexafluoro­phosphateACS reagent grade, Sigma-Aldrich Chemical no. 216593, or equivalent
Phosphoric acid 85 %e.g. Merck no. 1.00573, or equivalent
Phosphate buffer solution (pH 3.0 ± 0.1)Add 1.7 g of potassium dihydrogen phosphate, anhydrous into 1 L of water and mix to dissolve. Adjust this solution to pH 3.0 ± 0.1 with phosphoric acid. Add 8.0 g of ammonium hexafluorophosphate (NH₄PF₆) and mix well to dissolve.
NoteIt is recommended to filter this final solution through a 0.45 µm filter.
SolventWater + acetonitrile + phosphoric acid 900 + 100 + 1 (v/v/v) e.g. Pipette 1.0 mL of phosphoric acid into 900 mL of water, add 100 mL of acetonitrile and mix well.
Equipment
ApparatusSuitable HPLC system equipped with a pump, auto-sampler, UV detector capable of monitoring absorbance at 218 nm and a column heater.
ColumnWaters, Atlantis, dC₁₈, 3 µm, 100 Å
Length 150 mm, internal diameter 4.6 mm, or equivalent column
Filter for test solutionNylon 0.45 µm pore size, Titan or equivalent
Chromatographic conditions
Mobile phase APhosphate buffer solution + water 400 + 600 (v/v) Mix together 400 mL of phosphate buffer solution and 600 mL of water.
Mobile phase BPhosphate buffer solution + acetonitrile 400 + 600 (v/v) Mix together 400 mL of phosphate buffer solution and 600 mL of acetonitrile.
Mobile phase CMobile phase A + Mobile phase B 550 + 450 (v/v) or Phosphate buffer solution + water + acetonitrile 400 + 330 + 270 (v/v/v)
Isocratic conditionsMobile phase A: 55 % Mobile phase B: 45 % or Mobile phase C: 100 %
Column temperature40°C
Flow rate1.8 mL/min
DetectionUV, 218 nm
Injection volume10 µl of the test and reference solutions, equivalent to about 2.5 µg of Sakuramil drug substance in the reference solution
Run time3 minutes
System suitability test (SST)
SST solutions
·         Blank chromatogramSolvent
·         RepeatabilityReference solution
·         Tailing factorReference solution
Requirements
Blank chromatogramNo interfering peak at the retention time of Sakuramil drug substance in the chromatogram
RepeatabilitySrel ≤ 2.0 % (peak area of Sakuramil drug substance in the reference solution, n = 6)
Tailing factorT ≤ 2.0 (peak of Sakuramil drug substance in the first injection of the reference solution)
NoteCalculations in accordance with Ph. Eur. 2.2.46 “Chromatographic Separation Techniques” or USP <621>, “Chromatography, System Suitability”. Adjustments of chromatographic conditions to meet the system suitability requirements may be necessary.
ProcedureSelect not less than 30 units. Individually test 10 units (film-coated tablets or cores respectively). If the requirements are not met, continue testing to level 2 (or further units).
Test stock solutionPlace 1 unit into a 200 mL volumetric flask. Dilute to volume with solvent, stir for 45 minutes with a suitable magnetic stir bar. Centrifuge a portion of this suspension in order to get a clear supernatant or filter through a 0.45 mm Nylon filter (Titan or equivalent), discarding the first 3 mL of filtrate.
Test solution (for Sakuramil)Use test stock solution “as is”. (Conc. = 0.25 mg Sakuramil/mL).
NoteAlternatively a qualified dilutor system can be used, provided the resulting concentration lies within the validated range.
Test solutions are stable for 3 days, if stored at ambient conditions.
Reference solutionWeigh about 25 mg of Sakuramil drug substance, accurately to 0.01 mg, reference substances into a 100 mL volumetric flask, dissolve in and dilute to volume with solvent. Mix well.
NoteThe reference solution is stable for 9 days, if stored at ambient conditions or in a refrigerator.
EvaluationDetermine the peak area for Sakuramil in the chromatogram of test solution. Also determine the peak area for Sakuramil in the chromatogram of the reference solution.
Calculation for SakuramilPercent content, CUV, of Sakuramil, based on the declared content (= individual contents xi)

$$CUv = \frac {PATV × mRV × VT × CRV}{PARV × VR × mDV}$$

Where:

PATVPeak area of Sakuramil in the chromatogram of test solution
mRVMass of Sakuramil reference substance in mg
VTVolume of the test stock solution in mL (200)
CRVDeclared content of Sakuramil reference substance in percent
PARVPeak area of Sakuramil in the chromatogram of the reference solution
VRVolume of the reference solution in mL (100)
mDVDeclared Sakuramil content in mg per unit (50)

3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description

Principle       Near infrared absorption spectrometry (NIR method)

Equipment
ApparatusBruker FT-NIR equipped with accessories for external transmission tablet measurement, OPUS software (version 6.5 or higher).
Data acquisition settings**
Resolution32 cm⁻¹
Sample scan time128 scans
Background scan time128 scans
Save data fromat least 12500 cm⁻¹ to 6000 cm⁻¹
Result spectrumAbsorbance
Source setting**High intensity
Beam splitterQuartz
Aperture settingOpen (sample measurement), Reference spectralon (background measurement)
Measurement channelExternal transmission
Background measurement channelExternal transmission
Detector settingRT-InGaAs (external)
Scanner velocity**10 KHz
Acquisition modelDouble Sided, Forward-Backward
Phase correction modeMertz
Apodization functionBlackman-Harris 3-Term
Zero filling factor2
Signal gain, sample and backgroundAutomatic
Pre-amplifier gainSample measurement: B*) (equivalent to 1 in the audit trail)
Background measurement: Ref
*) recommended settings which might be adapted according to the performance of the instrument
**Settings can be adapted based on the type of the instrument
Calibration (data processing) parameters
Calibration method filename20_SakuraBloom_VX.q2 (X = current version 1, 2,…) Updated versions of the QUANT method will be named as follows: 20_SakuraBloom_CCNN_X.q2 (CCNN = site, X = current version)
For PLS model parameters refer to the associated validation and transfer report
System suitability test (SST)
Performance qualification (PQ) testingThis PQ must be performed and passed daily before any GxP acquisition, for the specific measurement channel (i.e. external transmission) to be used that day.
NIR test procedure
Collect the NIR spectraPlace the tablet holders (customized for Sakura Bloom uncoated core tablet of 20 mg dosage strength) in the automated sample wheel, and load the samples to be tested properly in the tablet holders.
The spectrum for each test tablet is collected following the acquisition of the background spectrum from the empty reference position on the sample wheel.
Select not less than 100 uncoated core tablets for testing. The exact number is dependent on the batch size and the related compression run time, which allows for an at-line assessment of the content uniformity in real time.
Quantification analysisThe measured NIR spectra are evaluated by the QUANT method mentioned above and single results for each tablet with the associated Mahalanobis distance is calculated.
Statistical Spectral Quality TestThe Mahalanobis distance limit is used automatically by the software to determine whether the characteristics of the sample fall within the range of variation for which the model was calibrated and validated.
Acceptance criteriaIn accordance with Ph. Eur. 2.9.47, Alternative 1 “Demonstration of uniformity of dosage units using large sample sizes”.

3.2.DP.M.1 Description of manufacturing process

1 Representative description of manufacturing process

Pre-Blending

• Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate/Lactose hydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance into a diffusion mixer (bin blender).

• Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

Granulation and blending

• Load the pre-blended material from Step 1 into a fluid bed granulator and add granulation liquid from Step 2 using an inlet air volume of 40-45 m³/min, an inlet air temperature of 75-85°C and a spray rate of 900 – 1100 g/min, to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules.

• Dry the obtained granules using dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit with inlet air temperature ranging between 75-85 °C until loss on drying of 1 - 2% is achieved.

• Sieve the dried granules from Step 4 using a screening mill.

• Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen (screen size 0.85 mm) and add it to the granules from Step 5.

• Blend the mixture from step 6 for 20 revolutions during 10 min using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

Tablet compression

• Compress the final blend from step 7 using a tablet press at 20-30 revolutions with a compression force of 6-14 kN to obtain the tablet cores.

Film coating

• Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water in a suitable sized vessel.

• Film-coat the tablet cores from Step 8 using the film coat suspension from Step 9 in a coating pan using an inlet air temperature of 70 - 80 °C, inlet air volume of 40-45 m³/min and a pan rotation speed of 2.0-6.0 rpm at stable conditions with a gradual increase of set target spray rate from 280 to 420 g/min. Collect the film coated tablets in a suitable container.

Inspection

• Collect 10 tablets to perform Description test method with RTRT and Identification Test method with RTRT.

Packaging

• The film-coated tablets are either primary packaged.

• The primary packaged product is then packed in a cardboard based secondary pack.

1. Summary

The manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets has been validated using three production-scale batches which have been processed in the same manufacturing facilities, using the same process and the same equipment as for the batches intended for marketing.

All three batches consistently meet the quality control specifications. The results of routine and extended in-process control (IPC) testing have demonstrated that the manufacturing process is robust and consistently yields a product capable of meeting the pre-defined quality characteristics.

Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets are produced according to standard manufacturing processes: Wet granulation, milling, drying of granulates, blending, mixing, compression and film-coating and is controlled by process parameter settings and in-process control testing performed during the manufacture. 9 Conclusion

The data gathered during the process validation show that the manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets is robust and consistently yields drug product which meets the predetermined quality characteristics. Moreover, the chosen in-process tests have been shown to be suitable for monitoring the manufacturing process.

The conclusion from the presented data is that the process conditions and values chosen for the processing parameters are acceptable to support the commercial manufacture of the product.

CQAs of Sakura Bloom Tablets are ensured by CMAs that are maintained by routine production. The control strategy in production of Sakura Bloom Tablets operates the following maintenance program to verify the model.

Daily check:

• Trend analyses of CQA and CMA are performed for every batch produced, and the changes are confirmed to be within an acceptable range.

• If the trend is out of the acceptable level, a comparison is made between the model and conventional testing methods. If the model has some problems, it should be revised. If the model has no problems, the relationship between CPP and CMA is considered to be broken. Thus, control of CPP is reviewed so that CMA has an appropriate value.

Periodical check:

• A comparison is made between the values calculated by the model and those obtained by the conventional testing methods at a certain production interval. If the difference between the two is out of the acceptable level, the model should be revised.

1 Potentially mutagenic impurities – ICH M7 Risk Assessment

Risk Assessment has been carried out according to ICH M7 guideline including classification of impurities with respect to mutagenic and carcinogenic potential based on literature data or in silico (Q)SAR assessment of impurities (using DEREK Nexus, SARAH Nexus). Results are provided in table below.

CP-6 (including enantiomer and diastereomer) and CP-4 (including enantiomer) have been tested positive in both (Q)SAR systems. The intermediate CP-5 and precursor intermediate CP-3 (non-isolated intermediates) exhibit positive structural alerts in a structure activity relationship database with the same aniline functionality. However, due to design of the manufacturing synthesis, these three intermediated and CP-4 are reacted in Step 3 to eliminate the aniline functionality responsible for the potential mutagenic characteristics. The reactivity of these potentially mutagenic impurities and intermediates together with the hydrophobicity of formed CP-7 and CP-9 (Sakuramil), in addition to, the Steps 3 and 4 crystallizations have excellent purge of the resulting unreacted drug aniline and byproducts, have consistently enabled control of these potentially mutagenic impurities in Sakuramil drug substance to a total of four (CP-6, CP-5, CP-4 and CP-3) of ≤ 37.5 ppm (37.5 ppm is the concentration limit of potentially mutagenic impurities of Sakuramil based on the highest dose). Concentration limit is calculated by dividing TTC by Maximum daily dose. TTC value is 1.5 µg/day as per ICH M7 guideline. Maximum daily dose of Sakuramil is 40 mg (= 0.04 g).

The aniline group that is responsible for the mutagenicity is classified by IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) as Group 3 according to ICH M7 guideline with a lifetime permissible daily exposure (PDE) of 720 µg/day.

Solvents, inorganic acids or salts are not covered by this risk assessment as these are controlled by other ICH guidelines.

1.1 Methodology

Hazard assessment of impurities in the Sakuramil synthesis involved:

• Initial analysis of actual and potential impurities by conducting database and literature searches for carcinogenicity and bacterial mutagenicity data

• Classification of impurities with respect to mutagenic and carcinogenic potential based on literature data

• (Q)SAR assessment of impurities for which literature data are not available using

• DEREK Nexus (Lhasa Ltd.)

• SARAH Nexus (Lhasa Ltd.)

• Classification of impurities with respect to mutagenic and carcinogenic potential based on (Q)SAR predictions and expert knowledge

The Risk Assessment considers the potential presence of nitrosamine impurities in Sakuramil drug substance based on the manufacturing process as defined in section [[2.3.3.DS.M Manufacture (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]].

The risk evaluation is performed using quality risk management principles, as outlined in ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management guideline.

The risk assessment has evaluated the following items as potential sources of nitrosamines or their precursors in line with root causes described in EMA/409815/2020.

Risk factors related to the manufacture of the active substance:

• Use of nitrite salts and esters (e.g. NaNO2, alkyl nitrites), or other nitrosating agents (e.g. nitroso halides, nitrosonium salts, nitrogen oxides, nitro alkanes, halogenated nitro alkanes, Fremy’s salt, nitroso sulfonamides), in the presence of secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process. Sources for secondary or tertiary amines can also be starting materials, intermediates, reagents, solvents (e.g. DMF, DMAc and NMP) and catalysts, which contain amine functionality, amine impurities (e.g. quaternary ammonium salts) or which are susceptible to degradation to reveal amines.

• Nitrite formation by oxidation of hydroxylamine or nitrite release from nitro-aromatic precursors (e.g. by fluoro de-nitration), in the presence of secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process.

• Use of disinfected water (chlorination, chloro-amination, ozonisation) in the presence secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process.

• Oxidation of hydrazines, hydrazides and hydrazones by hypochlorite, air, oxygen, ozone and peroxides in the manufacturing process or during storage

• Use of contaminated raw, recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) in the API manufacturing process.

• Use of contaminated starting materials and intermediates supplied by vendors who use processes or raw materials which may contain residual nitrosamines or nitrosating agents.

• Carry-over of nitrosamines deliberately generated (e.g. as starting materials or intermediates) during the manufacturing process.

Risk factors also related to finished product:

• A particular risk of formation of nitrosamines should be noted for active substances that contain a nitrosatable amine functional group. Several examples have been reported where the amine functionality was shown to be vulnerable to nitrosation and formation of the corresponding N-nitroso impurity (i.e. NO-API). Secondary amines appear particularly vulnerable to this reaction, although some cases with tertiary amines have also been observed.

• Does the API, or one of its known impurities, have a nitrosatable nitrogen functionality?

• May nitrites be present in one of the used excipients?

• Degradation processes of active substances, including those induced by inherent reactivity (e.g. presence of nitro-alkyl, oxime, or other functionality) or by the presence of an exogenous nitrosating agent.

• Oxidation of hydrazine or other amine-containing functional groups present in active substances or their impurities/degradants (e.g. from hydrazones and hydrazides), either in active substance manufacturing processes or during storage.

• Use of certain packaging materials.

• Reaction of amines leaching from quaternary ammonium anion exchange resins (e.g. used for purification steps) with nitrosating agents present in the liquid phase. In addition, disinfection procedures such as e.g. chlorination, chloro-amination and ozonisation can lead to significant N-nitrosamine generation as by-products in case vulnerable amines are present. Given the source of contamination, risk is related to the concentration of the reactive agent(s) and thus, to the volume of water in or used to dilute a particular product. The same risks could be associated with active substances or finished products manufactured using water purified using similar resins.

Risk factors related to GMP aspects:

• Cross-contamination due to different processes being run successively on the same manufacturing line.

• Carry-over of impurities between process steps due to operator-related errors or insufficiently detailed batch records such as inadequate phase separations during work-up procedures.

• Use of contaminated recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) where the recovery is outsourced to third parties who are not aware of the content of the materials they are processing. Recovery processes carried out in non-dedicated equipment should also be considered.

[IMAGE: Untitled.png]

In the proposed manufacturing process of SM2 CP-8 (1-bromo-3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)benzene) is prepared in a two-step synthesis starting from Br2. In the second step NaNO2 is used as a reagent to generate CP-8 from the intermediate 2-bromo-4-fluoroaniline HBr. The manufacturer from CP-8 Starting Material confirmed that vulnerable amines and vulnerable amine precursors are not used in the SM2 synthesis, therefore the risk for formation of N-nitrosamines and contamination of SM2 with nitrosamines is negligible. Nevertheless, since sodium nitrite is used it has to be assessed if some residual nitrite might be present in SM2 CP-8 and carried over into the Sakuramil drug substance manufacturing process. Considering the route of synthesis, there is no secondary or tertiary amine to form N-nitrosamine impurities in presence of sodium nitrite. Primary amines like the intermediate 2-bromo-4-fluoroaniline HBr are not capable of formation of N-nitrosamine in presence of sodium nitrite. Furthermore, considering the route of synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance after introduction of CP-8 (Step 4), there is a basic condition at low temperature of 12-25 °C. Both conditions do not support formation of N-nitrosamine impurities. Therefore, the overall risk is for formation/presence of nitrosamines due to SM2 CP-8 is evaluated as negligible.

[IMAGE: Untitled.png]

SM 1 CP-4 contains vulnerable amine. As there is no source of nitrites in Step 1 of Sakuramil manufacturing process there is no risk for formation of corresponding nitrosamine. However, in step 2 CP-5 intermediate, containing vulnerable amine moiety, is converted to CP-6 (also vulnerable amine). In this stage water is used under acidic conditions therefore risk for formation of the corresponding nitrosamines from CP-5 and CP-6 can not be fully excluded. Nevertheless, it is expected that potential nitrosamine of CP-5 would be converted during Step 2 to nitrosamine of CP-6. Therefore, it can be assumed that the levels of nitroso-CP-6, if present, would be significantly higher, than the levels of nitroso-CP-5 and therefore, only nitroso-CP-6 is relevant for further mitigation.

In conclusion, there is a potential risk for nitroso-CP-6 formation in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance, therefore testing of final drug substance batches is needed.

9 Degradation processes of active substances, including those induced by inherent reactivity (e.g. presence of nitro-alkyl, oxime, or other functionality) or by the presence of an exogenous nitrosating agent.

□ Yes

10 Oxidation of hydrazine or other amine-containing functional groups present in active substances or their impurities/degradants (e.g. from hydrazones and hydrazides), either in active substance manufacturing processes or during storage.

□ Yes

□ No

Justification: Oxidation of hydrazine or other amine-containing functional groups are not present in Sakuramil final drug substance.

11 Use of certain packaging materials.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

■ N.A.

Justification: No certain packaging materials are used.

12 Reaction of amines leaching from quaternary ammonium anion exchange resins (e.g. used for purification steps) with nitrosating agents present in the liquid phase. In addition, disinfection procedures such as e.g. chlorination, chloro-amination and ozonisation can lead to significant N-nitrosamine generation as by-products in case vulnerable amines are present. Given the source of contamination, risk is related to the concentration of the reactive agent(s) and thus, to the volume of water in or used to dilute a particular product. The same risks could be associated with active substances or finished products manufactured using water purified using similar resins.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

Justification: No quaternary ammonium anion exchange resins are used. No disinfection procedures are applied. Therefore, the risk for the formation of nitrosamines due to this root cause is considered as not applicable.

Risk factors related to GMP aspects

13 Cross-contamination due to different processes being run successively on the same manufacturing line.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

Justification: There is no risk on cross-contamination with alkylamines, nitrite or nitrosamines due to the use of multipurpose equipment as adequate cleaning procedures according to ICH Q7: Good Manufacturing Practice Guide for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients are in place. Therefore, the risk for the presence of nitrosamines due to cross-contamination due to the use of multipurpose equipment is considered as not applicable.

15 Use of contaminated recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) where the recovery is outsourced to third parties who are not aware of the content of the materials they are processing. Recovery processes carried out in non-dedicated equipment should also be considered.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

■ N.A.

Justification: Recovered or recycled materials are not used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance; therefore, the formation of N-nitrosamine impurities is not feasible.

3.2.DS.M.1 Description of Manufacturing process

Manufacturing process description for each process step along with corresponding CPPs, IPCs and their control ranges/acceptance criteria at each step are given below. Description includes also quantities of raw materials used.

Step 1 (CP-4 to CP-5)

CP-4 (175-185 kg), Methyl chloroformate (55-120 L) are combined. Lithium-tert-butoxide (22-85 kg) is added and stirred. To the mixture, tetrahydrofuran (750-920 L) is added and stirred. The layers are settled and separated. The resulting precipitates are filtered, rinsed with tetrahydrofuran and dried at temperatures up to 50°C to yield CP-5. Yield: Approximately 200 kg of Intermediate CP-5. About 91% in theory

Table 1-2: CPPs and IPCs of Step 1

N/AN/A
Step 2 (CP-5 to CP-6)

CP-5 (195-210 kg), Sodium borohydride (480-2120 kg), Magnesium chloride (22-35 kg) and methanol (105-320 L) are combined. Upon reaction completion, the mixtures is filtered, and to the filtrate hydrochloric acid (54-59 L) is added and stirred. The layers are settled and separated. The organic layer is concentrated by distillation with ethanol for the solvents exchange (final concentration 1000 L). Water (25 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol) is added and the mixture is stirred at 14 to 26°C. The resulting crystalline precipitates are filtered, rinsed with ethanol, and dried at temperatures up to 50°C to yield CP-6. Yield: About 235 kg of Intermediate CP-6, About 87% in theory

Step 3 (CP-6 to CP-7)

CP-6 (220-240 kg), tetrahydrofuran (598-3059 L), sodium carbonate (41.8-43.1 kg) are combined. Ethyl chloroformate (159-592 L) is added and the mixture is heated at temperature up to reflux. Upon reaction completion, the mixtures is filtered, and the filtrate is quenched with a sodium hydroxide solution (112-119 L) while maintaining a temperature below 30°C. To the mixture, n-hexane (52-55 L) is added and stirred, and then the layers are settled and separated. The organic layer is concentrated by distillation with ethanol for the solvents exchange (final concentration 1400L). Water (25 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol)is added and the mixture is stirred at 14 to 26°C. Step 4 (CP-7 and CP-8 to final drug substance)

CP-7 (240-260 kg) and CP-8 (200-220 kg)) are combined in methylene chloride (720-760 L). Tetra-n-butylammonium bromide (49-52 kg) and aqueous sodium hydroxide solution (720-760 L) are added while maintaining the mixture at temperatures between 12 and 25°C. Upon reaction completion, methylene chloride (805-815 L) and water (98-105 L) are added, the mixture is separated, and the organic layer is washed with diluted hydrochloric acid. The organic layer is concentrated and displaced by distillation with ethanol (final concentration 1800L). Water (20 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol) is added to the mixture. This addition of water in the crystallization is considered as CPP #4.1 with an acceptance range of 25 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol. Ethanol content is monitored by IPC #1. After cooling, the mixture is stirred at 14 to 26°C. Cooling rate is considered as CPP #4.2 with an acceptance criteria of 0.15 – 0.5 °C / min and tested in IPC #2. 3.2.DS.M.2 Development of manufacturing process and process control

1 Description of Critical Material Attributes from Starting Materials

1.1 Starting Material 1 - CP-4

CP-4 has been manufactured by IROHA-corp. (China) and HETO-corp. (Germany). CP-4 manufactured at commercial scale has been converted to Sakuramil drug substance that has been used in Phase 3 clinical trials and ICH drug substance stability studies. The quality of CP-4 is tightly controlled in accordance with the commercial specification in section [[2.3.3.SM.C Control [CP-4] [Sakuramil] [CP-6]]] .

Justification for section of CP-4 Starting Material is provided in section [[2.3.4.SM.D Description [CP-4][Sakuramil][CP-6]]].

The desired impurity profile of CP-4 is achieved through the use of a reproducible process and a robust crystallization using a combination of ethanol and water as the final solvent mixture.

All process related impurities present in the SM, CP-4, at levels greater than 0.1 % have been identified and appropriate limits and controls have been established based on demonstrated purge data, design space knowledge, and scale and equipment considerations in the subsequent synthetic steps. Individual unspecified impurities are controlled in lots of CP-4 to levels of NMT 0.5 %. CP-4 is not a source of impurities (≥ 0.15%) in the drug substance.

Stability evaluation of CP-4 has demonstrated that CP-4 is stable with no observations of significant degradation. An informal study of the stability of CP-6 under conditions of 30°C/65% RH through 18 months showed no degradation product increase or impurity change greater than 0.1 %.

1.1.1 Importance assessment for CP-4 material attributes

Fate and purge of related substances in CP-4 in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance is shown in the figure below.

CP-4 and CP-6 have tested positive in the Ames Assay. The intermediate CP-5 and intermediate precursor CP-3 exhibited positive structural alerts in a structure activity relationship database, therefore will be controlled as potentially mutagenic impurities (CP-4 and CP-6) as well.

Figure 1‑1      Fate and Purge of Related Substances in CP-4 in the Manufacturing Process of Sakuramil

[IMAGE: Untitled.png]

1.1.2 Control items for CP-4 high risk material attributes:

CP-4 is designated a high risk material attribute and the specification is established at NMT 0.3 % in the intermediate specification of CP-6. CP-4 is one of the four potentially mutagenic impurities in the process to manufacture Sakuramil drug substance; and all four of these impurities will be controlled in either the API specification or SM/Intermediate specification. It should be noted that CP-5 and CP-3 (two other potentially mutagenic impurities) are controlled under the unspecified impurity specification as NMT 0.1 % in CP-6 as shown in the table above. However, even at this level of 0.1 % for each of these two impurities, the level in Sakuramil drug substance for CP-5 and CP-3 is typically seen well below 1 ppm combined. The reactivity of the functional center responsible for the potentially mutagenic activity (aniline) combined with the purge factors for these two impurities is 100 times greater than in CP-4. In addition, 37.5 ppm was chosen as a target in Sakuramil drug substance based on the additive effect and combined control strategy for the last potentially mutagenic impurity: CP-6. This upstream critical control point for CP-4 is part of the combined control for all potentially mutagenic impurities as summarized below.

Summary of Potentially mutagenic Control Strategy

Control Strategy for CP-4, CP-5, CP-3:

In CP-6: Important MA CP-4 (≤ 0.3 %) + CP-5 and CP-3 (≤ 0.1 % each) = ≤ 10 ppm total for these three in Sakuramil drug substance as demonstrated by risk assessment outlined here [[2 Risk Assessment]] and supported by carry over studies in section [[ICH M7 Risk Assessment]].

Control Strategy for CP-6 (Intermediate):

< 10 ppm in Sakuramil when process through Steps 3 & 4 design space (specification for CP-6 as a CQA in Sakuramil drug substance: ≤ 25 ppm)

Therefore: CP-3 is controlled in CP-4 Starting Material specification, CP-4 is controlled in CP-6 Intermediate specification and CP-5 is controlled as unspecified impurity in CP-6 Intermediate specification as per Option 3. CP-6 is controlled in drug substance specification as per Option 1. Therefore it is ensured that all potentially mutagenic impurities are well controlled in accordance with ICH M7.

1.1.3 Control items for CP-4 moderate risk material attributes:

Identity, assay, unspecified impurities, and total impurities have not been identified as important material attributes.

However, they are important when managing current suppliers or evaluating additional supplier of CP-4. These tests serve as an opportunity to identify any potential new sources of impurities that were not possible to evaluate during the course of development. In addition, the downstream methods for CP-7 and for Sakuramil drug substance are excellent additional orthogonal methods used as well to manage and mitigate risk of unknown impurities introduced from CP-4.

1.1.4 Control items for CP-4 low risk material attributes:

The enantiomer (CP-4-E) is a low risk material attribute. As discussed above, chirality is controlled in the CP-2 and the process and intermediates have no impact on the chiral control. In addition, the process has significant purge of all isomers as well as methods that are specific for, and confirmed, the correct enantiomer of Sakuramil (specifications for intermediate and the drug substance are specific for all chiral isomers). Manufacturing of the enantiomer would therefore not go undetected early in the process. Nevertheless, enantiomeric purity is controlled within CP-4 specification as it is the next step after introduction of the “chiral pool” of CP-2.

1.2 Starting Material 2 - CP-8

While the starting material CP-8 exhibited positive structural alerts in a structure activity relationship database, it was determined to be negative in the Ames assay. The Ames report is attached in 3.2.DS.C. Therefore, CP-8 is controlled in Sakuramil drug substance as an unspecified impurity with a limit of NMT 0.10%.

CP-8 has been manufactured by IROHA-corp. (China) and abcr Gmbh. (Germany) using the same manufacturing processes. CP-8 manufactured at commercial scale has been converted to Sakuramil drug substance that has been used in Phase 3 clinical trials and ICH drug substance stability studies.

The quality of CP-8 is tightly controlled in accordance with the commercial specification in section [[2.3.3.SM.C Control [CP-8] [Sakuramil]]]

Justification for section of CP-8 Starting Material is provided in section [[2.3.4.SM.D Description [CP-8][Sakuramil]]]

All process related impurities present in the SM, CP-8, at levels greater than 0.1 % have been identified and appropriate limits and controls have been established based on demonstrated purge data, design space knowledge, and scale and equipment considerations in the subsequent synthetic steps. Individual unspecified impurities and total impurities are controlled in lots of CP-8 to levels of NMT 0.1 %. Related impurities CP-8-25l and CP-8-24l are controlled to levels of NMT 0.05%. CP-8 is controlled in the drug substance to the level of NMT 0.10%.

Stability evaluation of CP-8 has demonstrated that CP-8 is stable with no observations of significant degradation.

1.2.2 CP-8 important material attribute:

The two regio-isomeric benzylbromides are high risk material attributes as designated in the table above. The high risk material attribute justification is warranted due to the fact that they produce to isomers of the drug substance. These two isomers react mechanistically the same as the SM and have very little purge in the final crystallization to isolate Sakuramil drug substance.

Therefore, the specification (and thus the control strategy) is established as ≤ 0.05% for each to ensure the quality of Sakuramil drug substance.

1.2.3 Control items for CP-8 moderate risk material attributes:

Identity, assay, unspecified impurities, and total impurities have not been identified as important material attributes.

However, they are important when managing current suppliers or evaluating additional supplier of CP-8. These tests serve as an opportunity to identify any potential new sources of impurities that were not possible to evaluate during the course of development. In addition, the methods for Sakuramil drug substance are excellent additional orthogonal methods used as well to manage and mitigate risk of unknown impurities introduced from CP-8.

1.2.4 Control items for CP-8 low risk material attributes:

CP-8-OH and CP-8-CHO are not important material attributes. Both of these impurities do not react in the final step and have significant purge factors in the final isolation of drug substance. Fate and purge have demonstrated that 3 % is easily purged to ≤ 0.1 % unspecified level in drug substance.

The non important tests will be maintained within the purchase specification for CP-8 and the manufacturing sites quality systems.

2 Risk Assessment

2.1 Commercial manufacturing process related impurities (including intermediates and diastereomers)

All impurities that may be included in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance are shown in the following figure of Impurity cascade for Sakuramil.

All process related impurities present in CP-6 at level greater than 0.1% have been identified, and appropriate limits may be established based on demonstrated purge data in subsequent synthetic steps. Individual unspecified impurities are controlled in CP-6 to levels of NMT 0.1 %. CP-6 related impurities are not a source of significant levels of impurities in the drug substance. The desired impurity profile of CP-6 and Sakuramil are consistently achieved through a reproducible process and robust crystallizations. Because of the lipophilic nature of all the intermediates and Sakuramil (as a result of the trifluoromethyl functional group) the crystallizations have historically demonstrated an unprecedented, highly efficient purge of previous intermediates and impurities such that the quality of CP-6 and Sakuramil are historically independent of major and minor changes. This purge stands true for all process related impurities, diastereomers, potentially mutagenic intermediates, and starting material related impurities.

2.2.1 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Related substances

The following figure shows the impurities deriving from the manufacturing steps which could highly potentially impact CQA of Sakuramil. In step 3, ethyl homolog CP-7-1, the single impurity in the entire manufacturing process, is formed. CP-7-1 reacts and it converted to CP-9-1 in Step 4 and ultimately remains in the drug substance. CP-9-1 has very little purge in the crystallization in Step 4. Therefore, it is required to identify the process parameters which impact the formation and purge of CP-7-1 in Step 3.

In Step 4, unreacted SM CP-8 remains in the drug substance. Therefore, it is required to identify the process parameters which impact the formation and purge of CP-8 in Step 4.

SM CP-4, a potentially mutagenic impurity used in Step 1, is discussed in the section for potentially mutagenic impurities.

2.2.2 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Potentially mutagenic Impurities

SM CP-4, and CP-3, CP-5 and CP-6, potential impurities in SM, are potentially mutagenic impurities. It is required to investigate the process parameters which impact the purge of these impurities.

2.2.3 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Nitrosamine Impurities

Vulnerable amines are present in the drug substance, therefore it is required to investigate the risk on formation of N-nitrosamines. Nitrosating agents are not likely to be present in the drug substance.

2.2.4 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Chirality (Stereoisomers)

As stated in 1.2.6, no racemization has been observed in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance. As chirality is controlled in accordance with the vendor specifications of CP-2 as well as in the specifications of SM CP-4, and the manufacturing process and intermediates do not impact the control of chirality, it is not an important MA.

2.2.5 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Residual Solvents

Class 2 solvents THF, Methanol and n-Hexane are used in the manufacturing process, but because of several solid-liquid separation operations in the crystallization in Step 3 and Step 4, these solvents have not been detected in the development stage.

A Class 2 solvent dichloromethane is used in the reaction step in Step 4, but as it is designated to be submitted for crystallization after dichloromethane is evaporated after completion of the reaction, dichloromethane also has not been detected in the development stage. Therefore, it is not considered an important MA.

A Class 3 solvent Ethanol is used in all of the manufacturing steps (except Step 1) and it is defined a critical parameter as the content of Ethanol may influences the formation of ethyl homolog impurity (CP-7-1).

2.2.6 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Elemental impurities

Pd catalyst is used in the manufacturing process of the SM CP-4 in Step A. Therefore, Pd content has been included in the specification for SM as well as intermediate CP-6. As the level of metal does not increase in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance, it does not need to be controlled in final drug substance, however it is considered a important MA.

3 Design Space Development

For the purposes of defining the design space for the Sakuramil manufacturing process, the impact of the process on the critical quality attributes of Sakuramil was investigated in combination with quality risk management processes and tools. A design space for the commercial manufacture of Sakuramil has been established relative to its critical quality attributes and critical process inputs (material and process parameters). As there are no critical parameters in Step 1 and Step 2 that would not result in critical parameters in the final steps 3 and 4, this Design Spaces focuses on the final steps.

The following sections (Step 3 to Step 4) provide a summary of the risk based assessment of each step, the experimental work conducted, an assessment of the results and the resultant design space for each step, leading to the overall design space for the manufacturing process.

3.1 Focus area multivariate protocols, experimental summaries, and conclusions that set up the Design Space for Sakuramil drug substance

Introduction

Once the commercial route to Sakuramil was. established as described in the process development history section above, a greater understanding of the functional interrelationships of the manufacturing process parameters on the critical quality attributes of the dt.ug substance was established and this ultimately led to definition of the design space for the manufacturing process.

Initially, a risk assessment process was undertaken to identify all process parameters (including MA and in-process controls) and assess their probable impact on drug substance quality. In order to do this, each step of the manufacturing process was divided into focus areas (FA) and evaluated individually. Step 3 and Step 4 were each divided into FA1 - FA6. Evaluated FA are shown in Table 1-5. This initial risk assessment was conducted by means of Cause and Effect (C&E) Matrix. Examples of process parameters assessed are shown in Table 1-6.

First, the material attributes of the product for each step were assessed against their potential to impact a critical quality attribute of the dt.ug substance. Next, process parameters for each step were assessed against their potential to impact the important material att1·ibutes for that step product. The evaluation points were calculated and risks were classified into three levels (high, medium and low). This initial structured risk assessment utilized the knowledge that had been gained through development and scale up of the manufacturing process, and a mechanistic understanding of the chemistry of reactions and work up procedures.

The quality attributes that gain the highest priority to evaluate were the impurities generated and controlled by the process.

In Step 3, the aniline of CP-6 is reacted with ethyl chlorofo1mate to give the carbamate CP-7. Following the reaction, the mixture is quenched with a sodium hydroxide solution to consume any excess ethyl chlorofo1mate and hexane is added. The hexane layer is separated, exchanged with ethanol, and CP-7 is c1ystallized from an ethanol/water mixture.

Impurity quality attributes, parameters, and ranges for the Step 3 reaction study:

Only one impurity, ethyl homolog (CP-7-1 ), has been observed in batches of CP-7 that is fanned in the Step 3 process that could potentially impact this critical quality attribute of Sakuramil. This impurity is formed through the reaction of ethyl chloroformate with the nitrogen of the methyl carbamate; and then subsequent loss of the methyl carbamate (or loss of methyl carbamate and the alkylation with ethyl chloroformate). Step 3 is the source of CP-7-1 formation and it is the single impurity in the entire manufacturing process demonstrated to have little purge in the Step 3 and Step 4 crystallizations that give Sakuramil drug substance.

From the risk assessment, parameters that could potentially influence the levels of CP-7-1 (and total "other" impurities) in CP-7 were identified. This assessment identified that the stoichiometry of ethyl chloroformate and the base(s), and volume of THF were the process parameters that had the highest risk of impacting these quality attributes of CP-7. An experimental strategy was designed to determine the effects of this process parameter on controlling these quality attributes, improve process understanding and robustness, and establish the design space for the Step 3 manufacturing process.

Scale and equipment consideration: (Prior to multivariate design to establish the design space)

Neither the Sodium Carbonate particle size nor the agitation speed had any observable effect upon the reaction rate and product purity profile, indicating that poor mixing upon scale-up should not be a significant concern. Although the rate of the biphasic ethyl chloroformate quench is sensitive to agitation, there were no byproducts or safety concerns to indicate any potential issues upon scale-up related to mixing.

Through the course of development there has not been any observed scale and or equipment limitation, which is supplied by chemical knowledge. However, additional stressing experiments are executed to understand if there is any impact on prolonged time difference between laboratory and manufacturing times on the quality attributes. In addition, the multivariate experiments mimic the "worst case" scenario of the proposed commercial equipment and its limitations.

Note: The "worst case" scenario means the laboratory simulation of heating and cooling profiles, etc. of the worst conditions that may occur in the commercial manufacturing facility. For example, whether by-products or degradation products increase or not is confirmed by conducting the reaction at the temperature 10°C higher than the set reaction temperature or for a longer time than the set reaction time, or with reagents in a larger quantity than the set charge-in quantity.

3.1.2.1 Step 4 reaction

In Step 4, CP-7 is reacted with CP-8 in dichloromethane to give crude Sakuramil drug substance. The crude reaction mixture is quenched, extracted, and exchanged with ethanol; and Sakuramil drug substance is crystallized from an ethanol and water mixture.

Fate and purge data combined with reaction development indicate the level of CP-8 in the crude reaction mixture at levels of 1.2 % risk meeting the 0.10% specification in drug substance. Therefore, monitoring the reaction completion and using CP-8 as the limiting reagent must be seriously evaluated for criticality and control options. The risk assessment combined with prior development knowledge believes this is high risk to uncover multiple edges of failure and be a limiting factor of the design space.

MA of CP-8: A batch was chosen with the "high levels" of impurities in CP-8 for multivariate experimentation to highlight the ability of the design space to control impurities from this starting material. These data complement actual fate and purge data to help evaluate risk and determine acceptable levels and criticality.

Reaction:

In the reaction between CP-8 and CP-7, CP-8 is used as the limited reagent. A PAT method (REACTR) will be used in the reaction to evaluate the disappearance of CP-8. In addition, total "other" impurities were monitored while probing the ranges in the experimental design to identify if 1. Any new impurities are being generated, and 2. Any levels of known trace impurities already controlled in the standard process increase (< 0.1 %).

From the risk assessment, parameters that could potentially influence the levels of CP-8 (and total impurities) in drug substance were identified. This assessment identified that the stoichiometry of CP-8, phase ratio, and reaction concentration were the process parameters that had the highest risk of impacting the potential quality attributes of drug substance. An experimental strategy was designed to determine the effects of this process parameter on controlling these quality attributes, improve process understanding and robustness, and establish the design space for the Step 4 manufacturing process. NaOH concentration and TBAB catalyst eq. are non critical. Development range demonstrated no impact on quality or rate. Historical data / prior knowledge around phase transfer reactions are supports.

Scale and equipment consideration: (Prior to multivariate design to establish the design space)

As with many phase transfer reactions, the reaction rate will be severely impacted if the aqueous and organic phases are not adequately dispersed; however, product purity does not appear to suffer even after 24 hours under poor mixing conditions, indicating that the reaction is robust enough to withstand any mixing issues that may be encountered on scale ( e.g. temporary loss of agitation).

[IMAGE: Untitled.png]

Figure 3‑12    Relation between Agitation Rates and Reactor Temperature Profile
